newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian rupee seen dipping by two pct against dollar.
newsitem.headline: Indian rupee seen dipping by two pct against dollar.

text.p: The Indian rupee will weaken by a modest two percent against the dollar in the next six months, a Reuters poll of major banks and firms on Friday showed.
The survey of 24 banks and companies showed an average forecast for the rupee at 36.59 against the dollar by the end of July, down two percent from its current level of 35.85.
"On the macro level, the goverment has taken a lot of steps to increase dollar flows into the country," said V. Ravi Kumar, chief forex dealer at ABN AMRO Bank.
The government has relaxed norms for external commercial borrowings and is seeking to attract massive foreign direct investment to develop India's infrastructure sector.
Indian exports had lately shown a down trend, but so had imports, Ravi Pai, chief forex dealer at HDFC Bank, said.
This would help reduce the trade deficit, he said.

A dealer at a state-run bank said the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was unlikely to allow the rupee to fall steeply because of the government's ballooning oil subsidy account, which was expected to exceed 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) in 1996/97 (April-March).
"Allowing the rupee to fall now will aggravate the oil pool deficit in rupee terms," the dealer said.
The treasurer at a German bank in Bombay agreed that the RBI wanted to limit the rupee's fall.
"The rupee did not react on January 15," he said, referring to an outflow of over $200 million towards redemption of India Development Bonds to expatriate Indians on that day.
Payments of much lower amounts in the past have rocked the rupee as the Indian foreign exchange market is notoriously thin.
The second tranche of these bonds, expected to be close to $1.0 billion, will be redeemed on February 15.
"The RBI can easily spare $1.0 billion out of its reserves," said the banker.
India's foreign exchange reserves totalled $19.54 billion, the RBI said in a statement on January 15 after the redemption.
The rupee, which touched 35.95 against the dollar in December 1996, has tended to appreciate since January 1.
The RBI has been buying dollars to prevent the rupee's rise above the 35.85 a dollar level, dealers said.

Most bankers are bullish on the rupee, saying it will not weaken as much as it should if one considered the rising inflation rate and the appreciation of the dollar against other leading global currencies since December.

The survey showed the banks' and companies' average forecast for inflation, measured by the wholesale price index, of 9.14 percent annually by the end of the year, up from 7.75 at the end of the first week in January.
Some bankers and analysts said an inevitable correction in the rupee's exchange rate was only being postponed.
"The rupee needs to fall to 37.70 against the dollar by March 1997 to maintain its real exchange fair value," securities firm SocGen Crosby said in a January research report.
"The rupee has been appreciating against the mark, Japanese yen and French franc since December and the trend continues in January," said a dealer at a French bank.
This called for a correction in terms of faster depreciation of the rupee's value against the dollar, he said.
